extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and policymakers considering the ratification and design of the U.S. Constitution (voters and state officials)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical rules for structuring a republican constitution to maintain separation of powers, protect minority rights, and define representation and election rules. Covers remedies for departmental encroachments, internal institutional design, federalism, and qualifications/terms for the House of Representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional appeals to the people as remedy for departmental encroachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the people (occasional recourse) to determine meaning of the constitutional charter and redress encroachments between departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepts that appeals to the people are 'strictly consonant to the republican theory' for 'certain great and extraordinary occasions' but lists insuperable objections: (1) fails when two departments combine against the third; (2) frequent appeals imply defects and erode veneration for government; (3) stirs public passions and undermines dispassionate judgment; (4) legislative advantage (numerosity, local ties) biases outcomes; (5) conventions would be composed largely of parties and interested actors, producing partisan rather than reasoned results. Conclusion: occasional appeals are neither a proper nor effectual universal provision for keeping departments within constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical appeals (censorial revision) are generally ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, periodical appeals or a standing 'Council of Censors' to review constitutional infractions at fixed intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If review periods are short, they share the vices of occasional appeals; if remote, they produce feeble restraint and allow abuses to root. Empirical example: Pennsylvania Council of Censors (1783–84) exhibited party divisions, members who had been agents in the periods reviewed, biased deliberations, misinterpretations of departmental limits, and little practical effect on legislative practice. Excluding recently concerned persons would likely yield less capable or still partisan reviewers. Conclusion: periodical appeals are nearly as ineligible as occasional appeals for enforcing constitutional bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each department should have a will of its own
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure separate and distinct exercise of powers, each department must be constituted so its members have independent wills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should have 'as little agency as possible in the appointment of the members of the others.' Ideal (but not strictly required) construction: appointments for supreme executive, legislative, and judiciary drawn from the same popular fountain through unconnected channels. Practical deviations may be admitted for reasons like judiciary qualifications and tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal dependence of members of one department on others for emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of each department should be as little dependent as possible on members of the others for salary and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive or judges depended on the legislature for emoluments, their practical independence would be nominal. Financial independence is a core component of institutional autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply defenses by opposing interests: 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constitutional structures that give administrators personal motives and means to resist encroachments by other departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since human nature produces ambition, design institutions where private interests and rival ambitions act as sentinels over public rights; the interest of the officeholder should be connected to the constitutional rights of the place. This auxiliary precaution supplements dependence on the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide the legislature into different branches with different modes of election
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the legislative authority tends to predominate in republican government, it should be divided into branches chosen and acting differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Branches should be 'rendered... as little connected with each other as the nature of their common functions and their common dependence on the society will admit.' Division and differing electoral principles reduce legislative concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortify the executive by qualified connections rather than absolute negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive weakness may require strengthening by connections to weaker legislative branches rather than granting an absolute veto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An absolute negative may be unsafe (may not be exerted firmly on ordinary occasions or may be abused on extraordinary ones). Consider qualified connections between the executive and a weaker legislative branch so that the latter supports the constitutional rights of the executive without being detached from its own department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal compound republic provides a double security
rubrics_metrics.description: In a compound republic, power is divided between two governments (national and state) and then subdivided among departments within each, producing 'double security' for rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different governments control each other while each is self-controlled. This multiplicity of governments and subdivisions reduces the chance of consolidated tyranny and protects rights more than a single republic would.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of interests and sects protects minority rights; larger republic advantageous
rubrics_metrics.description: Security for civil and religious rights lies in multiplicity: many interests and sects make unjust majoritarian combinations improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods to protect minorities: create a will independent of the majority (risky) or enlarge the variety of interests so combinations are unlikely. In a large extended republic, the number and variety of interests mean coalitions of a majority would rarely be unjust; thus a larger practicable republic better secures self-government and minority rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the right of suffrage in the Constitution (electors' qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualifications of electors for the House are to match the electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures; the right of suffrage is a fundamental republican article and must be fixed by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving suffrage to Congress or to State legislatures would be improper: Congress regulation would be inadequate; leaving it to State legislatures would make the federal branch too dependent on states. The Convention's compromise—conform to state standards but fix them in the Constitution—was viewed as the best practical option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A Representative must be at least 25 years old; must have been seven years a citizen; must be an inhabitant of the State at the time of election; and during service must not hold any office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'reasonable limitations' open the federal House to merit of every description (native/adoptive, young/old) without regard to wealth or profession. They represent a considered, uniform federal standard for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency for the House: biennial elections secure dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections are the policy by which the House secures immediate dependence and sympathy with the people; biennial elections are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues by analogy and experience: British examples (historical triennial/ septennial shifts), colonial/state practice, and special circumstances of the federal government support that biennial elections sufficiently bind representatives to constituents without the dangers of annual returns. Additional points: the federal legislature holds only part of supreme legislative authority, will be checked by state legislatures, and will face less temptation from other branches—so biennial terms are safe and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of legislative terms should reflect degree of power
rubrics_metrics.description: Where greater power is conferred, shorter duration is generally appropriate; conversely, smaller power can permit longer terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the federal case: because the federal legislature has less comprehensive power than Parliament, somewhat longer terms are more defensible; nevertheless, for the House the balance of dependence favors biennial returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against annual elections framed as 'where annual elections end, tyranny begins' — context-sensitive proverb
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizes a common aphorism warning that annual elections protect liberty, but warns proverbs must be applied carefully to the particular institutional context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aphorism should not be mechanically applied; institutions differ and the appropriate frequency of elections depends on the balance between dependence on the people and other structural checks. (This entry anticipates nuanced treatment in continued discussion.)
